stances.claim: Article IX-C, Section 1, paragraph 2 of the Constitution requires presidential appointment with CA consent for a seven-year term, bars reappointment, limits replacement appointments to the unexpired term of the predecessor, and prohibits temporary or acting capacity.

An ad interim appointment is constitutionally permanent in nature because the term is fixed by law (until the next adjournment of Congress); the holder cannot be removed except for cause and after due process -- unlike temporary or acting appointees.

Garcia, Neri, and Pangarungan validly served and contributed to the peaceful and orderly conduct of the 2022 presidential elections; their appointments lapsed only because the CA bypassed them and Congress adjourned.

Under Funa v. COA (April 24, 2012), a commissioner who resigns with less than seven years served can be appointed chair for the unexpired portion of the departing chair's term -- provided the vacancy resulted from death, resignation, disability, or removal by impeachment. A promotional appointment is not barred by the no-reappointment rule.

Although Garcia did not 'resign' and the vacancy did not arise from one of Funa's four enumerated triggers, CA inaction can be considered equal to and 'in pari materia' with death/resignation/disability/impeachment -- so Garcia can validly serve as Comelec chair for the unexpired portion of Pangarungan's term, with total tenure capped at 7 years including his commissioner service.

Neri cannot be reappointed commissioner (express constitutional bar); she could be named chair but no longer can because the post is now occupied. Pangarungan cannot be returned to chair (now occupied and barred from reappointment to the same post) but could be a commissioner if appointed and he accepts.

Garcia's many former clients -- including the President, senators, representatives, governors, mayors -- are addressed by routine inhibition, a practice neither novel nor unethical; former SolGens promoted to the Supreme Court inhibit too when government cases are heard. The key is genuine inhibition plus desisting from influencing the remaining decision-makers.

one_paragraph_summary: A professor-reader asked Panganiban three questions about the ad interim appointment of George Garcia as Comelec chair: can it withstand constitutional scrutiny; should he have declined given his many clients with pending Comelec matters; and can Saidamen Pangarungan and Aimee Torrefranca-Neri be returned to the Comelec? CJ begins with Article IX-C, Section 1, paragraph 2 of the Constitution: presidential appointment with Commission on Appointments consent for a seven-year term, no reappointment, replacement appointments only for the unexpired predecessor's term, no temporary or acting capacity. Ad interim appointments, per settled jurisprudence, are permanent in nature (term fixed by law until the next adjournment of Congress); in February 2022, Pangarungan was named ad interim chair and Garcia and Neri ad interim commissioners -- all contributing to the peaceful and orderly 2022 elections -- but the CA bypassed them and their appointments lapsed at adjournment. Garcia was then given a second ad interim appointment, this time as chair. Funa v. COA (April 24, 2012) allows a commissioner who resigns with less than seven years served to be promoted to chair for the unexpired portion of the departing chair's term -- provided the vacancy arose from death, resignation, disability, or removal by impeachment -- because a promotional appointment (unlike a same-position reappointment) is not constitutionally barred. Although Garcia did not resign and the vacancy did not arise from one of the four enumerated triggers, CJ argues CA inaction can be considered 'in pari materia' with them, allowing Garcia to validly serve as chair for the unexpired portion, capped at seven aggregate years. Neri cannot be reappointed commissioner (express constitutional bar) and the chair is now occupied; Pangarungan cannot return as chair (no reappointment to the same post) but could be a commissioner if appointed and accepting. As to Garcia's many former clients including the President, senators, representatives, governors, and mayors -- inhibition is neither novel nor unethical; former Solicitors General promoted to the Supreme Court inhibit too. The obligation, however, extends beyond formal inhibition to 'desisting from influencing in any manner the remaining decision-makers.'
